title: Inquest hears shirt's blood a match on knife
article: Blood found on an Amherstburg police officer's golf shirt matches blood found on the knife Robert Scott Carpenter allegedly attacked him with, a DNA expert told a Coroner's inquest Monday.

Cecilia Hageman, assistant head of the biology section at the Centre of Forensic Sciences, testified she recently analyzed blood samples from both sides of the black-handled knife with a three-and a half inch blade.
Blood on one side of the blade matched the DNA profile of Carpenter, said Hageman. The odds of that blood belonging to someone unrelated to Carpenter are one in 16 trillion.

Blood analyzed on the other side of the knife was a mixture of DNA from at least two individuals, said Hageman. When Carpenter's blood was removed from the mix, the remaining sample matched the DNA profile of blood found on a blue-golf shirt belonging to Sgt. Bart DiPasquale.

The inquest probing the fatal police shooting last October of Carpenter, 36, has heard Carpenter attacked an unarmed DiPasquale with a knife and was shot once in the right femoral vein by Const. Shawn McCurdy. DiPasquale was out-of-uniform and wearing the golf shirt during the incident.

Carpenter's widow, Lisa Stewart, has alleged police planted the knife after the shooting. Her allegations were made public late in the day and the knife was only recently sent for testing. No identifiable fingerprints were lifted from the blade or handle.

Hageman could not say whether the blood on the knife matched the DNA profile of DiPasquale or any other Amherstburg police officer because no DNA samples, except for Carpenter's, were provided to her.
Jeff Rutherford, a use-of-force co-ordinator at the Ontario Police College in Aylmer, testified Monday that knives, even in the hands of small children, can be deadly.

He said chemical spray carried by police might not be effective in stopping a knife-threat because the attacker can fight through the spray. He added the spray would not be effective in confined spaces because of the risks of cross-contamination.

Rutherford said police officers and civilians experience "perceptual narrowing" during high-stress incidents, resulting in hearing impairment, tunnel vision, a decrease in co-ordination and the inability to remember details or track events as they occur.
Rutherford agreed with Andrew Bradie, lawyer for the officers involved in the shooting, that such effects could have caused Stewart to mistakenly identify DiPasquale as the shooter.
Dr. David Coates, Carpenter's family doctor for the three years preceding the shooting, agreed with Coroner's Counsel Robert Ash that Carpenter had a "constellation of problems" weighing him down.
The problems included chronic leg and back pain, depression, conflicts with Stewart, financial hardships and the repeated refusal of the Worker's Compensation Board to accept his disability claim.
A depression test administered to Carpenter last May indicated he was moderately depressed despite taking anti-depressants, said Coates.
